summary: Fourteen years after his first visit, Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, lays his Gentile mission before the respected leaders privately, and comes away with a handshake rather than a correction: Titus was not compelled to be circumcised, and the pillars asked only that the poor be remembered. Then, back in Antioch, Paul finds Peter withdrawing from eating with Gentiles under pressure from visitors, and opposes him to his face — and the rebuke becomes the letter's thesis: if righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing.
whyItMatters: This chapter is where the letter's argument becomes evidence: two incidents — an agreement and a confrontation — show that the one-Good-News claim of chapter 1 was tested publicly and held. The closing verses state the letter's heart in its most compressed form.

context.author: Paul, continuing the defense begun in chapter 1; the story is told as his own testimony, including his rebuke of Peter 'before them all.'
context.audience: The assemblies of Galatia, who are being told Paul's gospel is a secondhand and diluted version of Jerusalem's.
context.date: The chapter supplies its own clock — 'after a period of fourteen years' from the visit of 1:18 — while the correspondence with Acts is a live scholarly question (see the book briefing's debates).
context.setting: Two places: Jerusalem, where the private meeting with the respected leaders happens, and Antioch, where the confrontation with Peter occurs over shared meals.
context.literaryForm: Narrative testimony turning to direct speech: the chapter's argument peaks inside a quoted rebuke, so the reader hears the case the way the Antioch table heard it.

outline.heading: Up to Jerusalem by revelation, with a test case
outline.note: Fourteen years on, Paul presents the Good News he preaches among Gentiles privately to the respected; Titus, a Greek, is the case in the room — and is not compelled to be circumcised.

outline.heading: False brothers and an hour of subjection refused
outline.note: Intruding 'false brothers' wanted to spy out the liberty in Christ and bring them into bondage; Paul refused to be subjected 'not for an hour' so the truth of the Good News would continue with the Galatians.

outline.heading: The pillars add nothing; a handshake instead
outline.note: The respected ones imparted nothing to him; they recognized the entrusted commissions — Peter for the circumcised, Paul for the uncircumcised — and James, Cephas, and John gave the right hand of fellowship, asking only that the poor be remembered.

outline.heading: Peter at Antioch: the withdrawal
outline.note: When Peter came to Antioch he ate with Gentiles — until certain people from James arrived and he drew back, and the rest of the Jews joined the hypocrisy, including Barnabas.

outline.heading: The public rebuke and the letter's thesis
outline.note: Paul's question before them all — why compel Gentiles to live as Jews? — turns into the argument: not justified by works of law but through faith in Christ; crucified with Christ; 'if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing.'

keyVerses.text: yet knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the law, because no flesh will be justified by the works of the law.
keyVerses.why: The letter's central claim, stated inside the Antioch rebuke — and note it begins with 'we': Paul includes himself and Jewish believers in it.

keyVerses.text: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.
keyVerses.why: The argument becomes a person: the doctrine of 2:16 lands here as Paul's own life, and the 'who loved me' is why this verse became one of the most-quoted lines in the letter.

keyVerses.text: I don’t reject the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!”
keyVerses.why: The sharpest form of the letter's logic: adding law to the equation does not supplement Christ's death, it voids it.

themes: a meeting that changed nothing and confirmed everything
Titus uncircumcised as the test case
justified by faith, not works of law

questions.question: Why did Paul bring Titus to Jerusalem?
questions.answer: Titus was a Greek — a Gentile believer — and his presence made the question concrete rather than theoretical: would the Gentile believer be required to be circumcised? The chapter reports the outcome as evidence: 'not even Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised' (2:3).

questions.question: Why does Paul say he laid the matter before the leaders privately?
questions.answer: He says he presented the Good News 'privately before those who were respected, for fear that I might be running, or had run, in vain' (2:2). A private consultation could not become a public correction of him — the letter's point is that no such correction happened; the pillars added nothing to his message (2:6).

questions.question: Who were the 'false brothers secretly brought in'?
questions.answer: The letter identifies them only by their action: they 'stole in to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, that they might bring us into bondage' (2:4). Paul gives them no names and reports no debate with them — only that he refused subjection 'not for an hour.' Their position is the same one the Galatian agitators hold, which is why the story appears here.

questions.question: What did the Jerusalem leaders actually decide?
questions.answer: By Paul's report: nothing was added to his message (2:6); the commissions were recognized as parallel — Peter to the circumcised, Paul to the uncircumcised (2:7-8); and James, Cephas, and John gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship with one request — 'remember the poor' (2:9-10).

questions.question: What exactly was wrong with Peter's behavior at Antioch?
questions.answer: He had been eating with Gentiles — which the law's boundary markers made uncomfortable for Jewish observance — then withdrew when 'certain ones from James' arrived, and his example pulled the other Jews and even Barnabas into the same hypocrisy (2:12-13). The hosted text calls it hypocrisy because the behavior contradicted what Peter himself actually practiced: he 'lived as the Gentiles do.'

questions.question: What does 'justified' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: The word is courtroom language: to be counted or declared in the right before God. Paul's claim is that this standing comes 'through faith in Jesus Christ' and not 'by the works of the law' (2:16) — the chapter's own definition of works of law is visible in the Antioch story: the food and table boundaries being used as the entry price for Gentiles.

questions.question: 'Faith in Christ' or 'the faithfulness of Christ'?
questions.answer: The Greek phrase pistis Christou behind 2:16 (and 3:22) can be read either way, and the choice decides whether the emphasis falls on the believer's trust or on Christ's own faithfulness. The hosted World English Bible renders it 'faith in Jesus Christ,' one of the two live scholarly readings; the debate is not settled, so both are worth knowing about when comparing translations.

questions.question: How can Paul say 'I through the law died to the law'?
questions.answer: The sentence at 2:19 is compressed: the law itself pronounced the death sentence that ended Paul's obligation to it — he reads his own crucifixion with Christ (2:20) as that death, so that what lives now is Christ living in him. The argument is not lawlessness but a changed jurisdiction: he died to the law's claim in order to live to God.

questions.question: Is Paul saying the law is against Christ's death being enough?
questions.answer: The verse says the reverse implication: 'if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing' (2:21). Paul is not evaluating the law in the abstract here; he is testing a specific claim — that law-keeping is the path to being right with God — and saying that claim, if true, would make the cross unnecessary. The chapter leaves no room where both the law and the cross are needed for standing before God.

glossary.def: Counted or declared in the right before God; the chapter argues this comes through faith in Christ, not by works of the law.
In this chapter, the observances being required as the entry price for Gentiles — circumcision above all, and the table boundaries Peter obeyed at Antioch.
James, Cephas (Peter), and John — the Jerusalem leaders Paul names as those who gave him and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship (2:9).
